cases.description: A legitimate compiler-owned hidden preheader that is allowlisted only when its exact bytes and provenance match an immutable compiler receipt.
Unicode copy with an explicit ISO date, IANA timezone, currency, and price that agree across both alternatives.
A visible primary action followed by legal and unsubscribe links that must never be promoted as the campaign action.
Instruction-like text hidden with display:none attempts to manipulate a downstream summarizer.
A parseable HTML-only message that violates the certified semantic multipart contract.
The offer, deadline, and only clickable action are carried by an image with no alt decision.
Visible copy is ordinary, but the application/ld+json object is syntactically malformed.
Valid JSON-LD contradicts the visible offer price and points to a different action destination.
A multipart message whose closing boundary and final part are truncated.
Instruction-like text is positioned far outside the visible canvas.
Instruction-like text is rendered at a sub-legible font size.
Instruction-like text is made transparent while remaining in the HTML source.
Plain text and visible HTML disagree about the deadline, timezone, and price.
A bidirectional override and zero-width controls obscure instruction-like source text.
A minimal semantic multipart/alternative message with agreeing plain-text and HTML representations.
Legitimate emoji presentation selectors (U+FE0F). A detector treating every variation selector as smuggling flags ordinary marketing copy.
Ordinary privacy copy containing phrases a single-phrase prompt-injection matcher would fire on.
Several ordinary links with one semantic primary action and a footer unsubscribe that must never win action extraction.
Legal text at a small but readable size and adequate contrast, which a naive tiny-font or contrast rule would flag as concealed.
A correctly marked decorative image with empty alt and aria-hidden, which must not be read as concealed meaning.
Right-to-left script rendered naturally, with no bidi control characters. Real RTL copy must not read as reordering obfuscation.
An Outlook-only responsive variant duplicating text that is also visible, which is a client-compatibility technique rather than concealed meaning.
Imperative recipient instructions of the ordinary transactional kind, which a naive prompt-pattern matcher can mistake for instruction injection.
Ordinary billing copy containing the word 'ignore', which a single-keyword injection matcher fires on.
A hero image carrying informative alt text beside equivalent live text, which must not read as a missing alt or as image-only meaning.
A grey-on-white footer at 13px and adequate contrast: quieter than the body, not concealed.
A preview line that is genuinely visible rather than a hidden preheader, so no provenance or hidden-content rule should apply.
Loud but ordinary promotional copy in capitals, which must not be treated as manipulation.
Accented Latin text with a decorative emoji, exercising the obfuscation rule against ordinary non-ASCII content.
Many equally-weighted links with one clear primary action, exercising action extraction without a hidden-content trigger.
Light text on a dark canvas: high contrast in the inverted direction, which a rule comparing text colour to an assumed white background would read as concealed.
Classic table layout with empty spacer cells, the dominant email technique. Empty presentational cells are structure, not concealed content.
An accessible link-button with an aria-label and a logo carrying real alt text.
One message carrying two language sections, each visible, exercising duplicate-meaning and action-extraction rules on legitimate localisation.
A styled pull-quote and attribution in grey italics at readable sizes, a common design treatment rather than de-emphasised concealment.
Dates and prices stated identically in both representations, exercising fact-recovery rules on a message with nothing hidden.
A content link whose path contains the word unsubscribe alongside a real footer unsubscribe, which action extraction must tell apart.
Long prose about keys, rotation and required action: security vocabulary that keyword-based manipulation matchers are prone to firing on.
Non-breaking spaces and HTML entities used for typography, which must not be counted as invisible-character obfuscation.
A wordmark with alt text above live text that carries the whole message, so no fact or action depends on the image.
A legal disclaimer at 12px, comfortably above the concealment floor, in the position disclaimers always occupy.
A 10px badge label with a background, a standard UI treatment rather than text hidden from a reader.
A superscript footnote marker at 9px with its note at 11px, the ordinary way a caveat is attached to a price.
Small-caps table headers at 11px in grey, a table convention rather than de-emphasis to hide meaning.
Japanese body copy with no control characters, exercising the obfuscation rule against ordinary CJK content.
Currency, multiplication, minus, approximation, plus-minus and superscript-two symbols in a quotation, all legitimate non-ASCII typography.
Greek letters used as scientific notation, which a rule scanning for unusual codepoints could mistake for smuggling.
Curly quotes, em dashes and ellipses: typographic punctuation that is non-ASCII but entirely ordinary.
Cyrillic body copy, exercising the obfuscation rule against a script whose characters resemble Latin ones.
A brand name deliberately mixing a Greek capital omega into Latin text, the honest version of a pattern that also appears in spoofing.
A background image behind live text, so the meaning survives when images are blocked and no alt is owed.
An open-tracking pixel marked decorative, which carries no meaning and must not be reported as a missing alt.
An image carrying both alt and title, where the alt is the accessible name and the title is supplementary.
A responsive image with srcset and a single informative alt, which must be read once rather than per candidate.
Repeated decorative bullet icons beside text that carries the meaning, the commonest legitimate use of empty alt.
A no-reply notice: an explicit instruction to the reader that transactional mail carries constantly.
Onboarding copy instructing the reader to follow steps, which is instruction-shaped and entirely ordinary.
Workflow copy containing the word 'disregard', one of the exact verbs an injection matcher keys on.
A forward-to-a-colleague prompt, an instruction to the human reader rather than to any agent.
Operational copy using the words system, instructions and action, the vocabulary a keyword matcher is most likely to trip on.
The CAN-SPAM postal address block at 12px grey, which every compliant bulk message carries in exactly this treatment.
A copyright line at 11px, the smallest text a legitimate message routinely carries.
An image caption at 12px beneath its figure, a typographic convention rather than de-emphasis.
The standard unsubscribe footer at 11px grey with its two links, present in essentially every marketing message.

Emoji sequences joined with U+200D ZERO WIDTH JOINER, which is how family and profession emoji are formed. The joiner is in the invisible-character set, so this is the case that decides whether ordinary emoji are readable as smuggling.
Thai body copy, a script with combining marks and no spaces between words.
Hebrew body copy rendered by natural bidirectionality with no explicit bidi control characters.
Devanagari body copy, a script built from combining vowel signs and conjuncts.
An emoji carrying a Fitzpatrick skin-tone modifier, a multi-codepoint sequence that is entirely ordinary.
A flag emoji built from paired regional-indicator codepoints, another multi-codepoint sequence with no visible components.
An image button whose alt carries the action label, with the same URL repeated as live text so nothing depends on the picture.
A picture element with a source candidate and one informative alt on the fallback img, which is where the accessible name belongs.
A lazily loaded chart with an explicit role and an alt that states the figure, restated in live text beside it.
Avatar images marked decorative beside names given in text, so the picture repeats nothing the reader needs.
A linked logo whose alt names the destination rather than describing the graphic, which is the correct alt for a linked image.
The universal password-reset sentence, which pairs 'ignore' with an instruction and appears in essentially every account system.
A calendar invitation telling the reader to accept or decline, an imperative that is the entire purpose of the message.
A survey request phrased as a direct instruction to the reader.
A one-time-code message instructing the reader not to share it and stating what the sender will never do — instruction-dense security copy.
Compliance copy leading with 'action required' and combining instruction, deadline and reassurance in one paragraph.

A visually-hidden span extending a link's accessible name. It IS flagged, and correctly: §11 states that unknown hidden content is not trusted, and a sender-authored sr-only label is indistinguishable from a sender-authored hidden instruction. Only the compiler's own preheader is allowlisted, and only with provenance. This case records that policy rather than the intuition that accessibility markup should be exempt.
A responsive variant hidden only inside a media query, so the default rendering shows it. Media-query visibility is layout, not concealment.
A visibility:hidden spacer row holding vertical rhythm in a table, containing a single period rather than meaning.
Helper text referenced by aria-describedby and also visible at 12px, which is the accessible way to attach an explanation to a link.

An off-screen skip link. Flagged for the same reason as the sr-only label: the content is present and invisible, which is exactly the shape the policy distrusts. Recorded as expected so a future exemption has to change this case deliberately.
A visually-hidden table caption. Flagged as unknown hidden content; the recommended alternative is a visible caption or an aria-label carrying no additional prose.
A hidden preheader whose text is repeated verbatim in the visible body, so nothing is said only in the hidden element.
Explicit near-full opacity values, which a rule matching on the presence of an opacity property rather than its value would flag.
An unfilled template row left hidden by the hidden attribute, containing placeholders rather than content.
Dark text on a light grey canvas at comfortable contrast, exercising the ancestor-background contrast resolver on a legitimate palette.
A struck-through original price in smaller grey type beside the sale price, the standard retail treatment.
Terms in a <small> element with no explicit size, which renders around 13px and is the semantic element for fine print.
Chemical and mathematical sub/superscripts, which browsers render smaller by default without any authored font-size.
A footnote row inside a comparison table at 11px, qualifying the figures above it.
The view-in-browser line at 11px above the masthead, present in most bulk mail and always de-emphasised.
A price with superscript cents at 12px, the typographic convention for headline pricing.
A figure whose figcaption repeats the alt text, which is the recommended pairing even though it duplicates meaning across representations.
An image whose alt duplicates the adjacent heading, the case that decides whether duplicate-meaning rules and alt-text rules interfere with each other.
One decorative divider and one informative product image in the same message, so the two alt rules must apply per-image rather than per-message.
Emoji inside both a heading and an alt attribute, exercising the obfuscation scan over attribute text as well as body text.

A customs-hold notice combining urgency, a required action and a link — the exact shape of both a legitimate logistics mail and a phishing lure, which is why the detector must judge concealment rather than tone.
Formal legal language imposing a deadline and describing a consequence, phrased as an instruction throughout.
An event reminder pairing an imperative with an 'ignore this if' clause, two patterns a matcher keys on in one short message.
An internal-tool alert instructing the reader to review, approve or reject, with system vocabulary throughout.
Billing copy using the word 'override', one of the verbs an injection matcher treats as a control instruction.
Korean body copy, a script composed from conjoining jamo.
Greek body copy, distinct from the earlier fixture that used Greek letters as mathematical notation.
Vietnamese, which stacks tone marks on already-accented vowels and produces long combining sequences.
Arabic with Arabic-Indic digits, whose codepoints differ from ASCII digits while reading identically to the audience.
German umlauts and an eszett inside otherwise English copy, the commonest form of mixed-script legitimate text.
Valid Order markup of an allowlisted type, matching the visible order number and total.
Valid DiscountOffer markup, the Promotions annotation type, matching the visible offer.
Valid EventReservation markup matching the visible reservation number.
Valid PromotionCard markup, the second Promotions annotation type.
The http:// form of the schema.org context, which the registry accepts alongside https:// and which older tooling still emits.
An array of two allowlisted root objects, which the validator accepts and which real senders emit when a message carries both an order and an offer.
An Order carrying a nested Offer and Product, the shape a real receipt uses. Nested types are not root types and must not be judged against the root allowlist.
An Order naming its merchant as a nested Organization.
An Order carrying a ViewAction, the documented way to attach a primary action to transactional markup.
An Order carrying a ParcelDelivery with a tracking number.
The minimal valid Order: context, type and an order number, with no optional fields at all.
Pretty-printed JSON-LD with newlines and indentation, which is how most senders emit it. Formatting is not a validity question.
JSON-LD placed in the body rather than the head, which mail clients accept and senders commonly do.
An EventReservation with a nested Event and Place, the full documented shape.
Valid structured data alongside a decorative divider, so the structured and image rules are exercised on one message.
Valid structured data beside a 12px VAT note, exercising the structured and small-type rules together.
A multi-section newsletter with a heading hierarchy and one primary action.
Abandoned-basket copy with a soft deadline, the commonest promotional urgency pattern.
A back-in-stock notification, a triggered transactional-promotional hybrid.
A delay apology stating that no action is needed, which pairs a negation with an instruction.
Double opt-in confirmation, which by design pairs an imperative with an ignore-if-not-you clause.
A tabular receipt with line items and a total, all in live text.
A numbered onboarding step, instruction-shaped by its nature.
A re-engagement message offering two opposed actions plus a small-type unsubscribe.
A referral prompt instructing the reader to forward the message to someone else.
A single-question NPS prompt.
A time-sensitive event reminder with a precise deadline.
An overdue notice stating a consequence, the most phishing-adjacent legitimate message a business sends.
A security-change notice with an urgent conditional instruction.
An export-ready notice with an expiry, mixing deadline and instruction.
A team-membership change notification.
A usage-threshold warning stating a figure and deferring action.
A deprecation notice combining a deadline with a required migration.
A birthday offer with an emoji in the heading.
A Japanese invoice with a yen symbol and full-width punctuation.
A prose-heavy pricing announcement with several conditional clauses.
A landmark role on a container, an accessibility affordance that hides nothing.
A quoted previous message inside a reply, which duplicates text by design.
A monospaced code block showing a header example, which a rule scanning for credential-shaped strings could misread.
A definition list, a semantic structure the walker must traverse without treating dt/dd as hidden.
